title: The Real Cost of the Pentagon’s Military Buildup in the Pacific
author: William Hartung
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/pacificfleet-680x327.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/13/the-
real-cost-of-the-pentagons-military-buildup-in-the-pacific/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/pacificfleet-680x327.png)

The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group. Photo: US Navy.

President Donald Trump and self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth are
pushing for a post-World War II record [$1.6
trillion](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1057526650105224 "$1.6 trillion")
Pentagon [budget](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/house-votes-to-adopt-
department-of-war-renaming-as-part-of-annual-defense-bill "budget") for next
year, a sum so obscenely high that it is almost impossible to comprehend. The
proposed $600 billion _increase_ alone is [almost
twice](https://chinapower.csis.org/military-spending/ "almost twice") the
_total annual military_ budget of America’s closest rival, China.

That supposed rivalry, despite the big spending gap, makes China central to
justifying the Pentagon’s bloated budget. And Hawaiʻi is, in turn, central to
the Trump administration’s Indo-Pacific military strategy which assumes that
deterring China requires a forward, offensive strike posture anchored by the
archipelago. This not only puts a target on Hawaiʻi — as was the case during
World War II, when Pearl Harbor was attacked by Japan — but it also deepens
long-standing economic hardships and environmental degradation produced by
more than a century of U.S. military occupation, according to “[The True Cost
of the U.S. Military in Hawaiʻi](https://ips-dc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/report_true_cost_of_us_military_in_hawaii.pdf "The
True Cost of the U.S. Military in Hawaiʻi"),” a new report by the Institute
for Policy Studies.

The report finds that as the Pentagon has shoved Hawaiʻi toward the front
lines of a potential nuclear conflict, it has also poisoned the islands’ land
and waters, lied about its economic benefits, tied Hawaiʻi’s financial well-
being to an inefficient use of tax dollars, and failed to pay more than $130
billion in back rent. And now the Trump administration is extending its
buildup in Hawaiʻi — which has long “been central to the architecture of U.S.
imperial power” to expand facilities, build new bases, and secure access to
air and naval bases from Guam to the Pacific island chain to the Philippines
to Australia. And these moves in the Pacific are just one part of that
multifaceted $600 billion boost being sought for the Pentagon.

**The China Syndrome**

In addition to greed, grift and pork-barrel politics — practices that have
reached an astonishing level due to the [unapologetic
corruption](https://delauro.house.gov/CorruptDon "unapologetic corruption")
and feverish [insider dealings](https://oversightdemocrats.house.gov/trump-
family-corruption-tracker "insider dealings") of the [Trump
family](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/13/gillibrand-crypto-trump-profit-
clarity-act/ "Trump family") and its hangers-on — the biggest driver of the
Pentagon’s enormous budget is America’s quest for unrivaled global military
dominance. At the center of that effort are preparations to “win” a [war with
China](https://theintercept.com/2023/02/03/china-americas-frontier-fund/ "war
with China"), a mission that is likely impossible and would be extremely
dangerous to undertake.

The probable outcome of a war with Beijing — which is, after all, a
sophisticated technological power armed with nuclear weapons — would be
unprecedented [devastation for all
concerned](https://carnegieendowment.org/podcasts/the-world-unpacked/how-a-us-
china-war-would-unfold "devastation for all concerned"), especially the people
of Taiwan, the independent island nation of the coast of the mainland that
China considers a breakaway province. Hawai‘i, Guam, and the other launching
pads for a U.S. military operation against China would undoubtedly be targets,
with dire consequences for the residents of those islands.

Well before recentering China as national security adversary No. 1, America’s
quest for military supremacy was not going well, to put it mildly.

As the Costs of War Project at Brown University has
[shown](https://costsofwar.watson.brown.edu/ "shown"), America’s post-9/11
wars have been an unmitigated disaster, costing or causing long-term
obligations of an astonishing [$8
trillion](https://theintercept.com/2021/09/01/war-on-terror-deaths-cost/ "$8
trillion"), as well as the deaths of hundreds of thousands of civilians and
the displacement of tens of millions more, Meanwhile, these wars [failed
miserably](https://theintercept.com/collections/the-911-wars/ "failed
miserably") in meeting their stated objectives, leaving in power a sectarian
regime in Iraq that opened the door to the rise of ISIS and a [Taliban-
led](https://theintercept.com/2021/08/26/afghanistan-america-failures/
"Taliban-led") government in
[Afghanistan](https://theintercept.com/2021/08/17/afghanistan-papers-kabul-
taliban-craig-whitlock/ "Afghanistan"), a status quo ante bellum after more
than 20 years of war.

It’s hard to envision a more complete mismatch between stated war aims and
real-world results than the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, until we take a hard
look at the [illegal](https://action.aclu.org/send-message/war-on-iran
"illegal"), immoral, and ill-conceived [conflict with
Iran](https://theintercept.com/2026/06/11/trump-iran-war-claims-failures/
"conflict with Iran") which is fast becoming a [new forever
war](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/17/trump-iran-war-cost/ "new forever
war").

Despite this dismal record, the Trump regime — and the Biden administration
before it — has chosen to double down on a military-first foreign policy, with
the demonization of China fueling the fire.

The Pentagon refers to China as the “[pacing
challenge](https://www.pacom.mil/Media/NEWS/Article/2846904/china-remains-
pacing-challenge-for-us-pentagon-press-secretary-says/ "pacing challenge"),”
even as military spending far outpaces Beijing’s defense budget. And in its
most recent assessment, the Pentagon outlined a strategy to [cow China into
submission](https://media.defense.gov/2025/Dec/23/2003849070/-1/-1/1/ANNUAL-
REPORT-TO-CONGRESS-MILITARY-AND-SECURITY-DEVELOPMENTS-INVOLVING-THE-PEOPLES-
REPUBLIC-OF-CHINA-2025.PDF "cow China into submission") by “being so strong
that aggression is not even considered.”

China hasn’t been involved in a major shooting war since the much smaller
nation of Vietnam fought it to a virtual standstill in 1979, nearly five
decades ago. China’s forces “[severely
underperformed](https://www.businessinsider.com/what-china-war-with-vietnam-
means-for-its-next-war-2021-3 "severely underperformed")” in the one-month
conflict; according to one account, “PLA soldiers were so undertrained that
there were reports of infantrymen tying themselves to tanks with ropes to
avoid falling off, sealing their fate when they were ambushed.”

Presumably Chinese forces are much better trained now, but China is not a
serial aggressor, and although it has engaged in border skirmishes with India,
it has not been embroiled in virtually [nonstop
conflicts](https://fletcher.tufts.edu/research/research-
publications/introducing-military-intervention-project-new-dataset-us-military
"nonstop conflicts") over the past half century, as the United States
[has](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/30/trump-secret-wars/ "has"), nor has
it fought regime-change wars. So the question arises: Who is setting the pace
in the U.S.–China arms race, Washington or Beijing?

**Two Systems, Two Countries**

In the real world, China’s military is not 10 feet tall, and throwing more
money at the Pentagon is the worst possible way to address the greatest
challenges posed by Beijing, which are actually not military in nature.

China’s vast global influence leans heavily on its economic clout, which is
built on aid and trade, including the [Belt and Road
Initiative](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/chinas-massive-belt-and-road-
initiative "Belt and Road Initiative"), a globe-spanning collection of
interconnected infrastructure projects. (To be clear, the Belt and Road has
too often involved [dubious
deals](https://revolve.media/features/shortcomings-of-chinas-belt-and-road-
initiative "dubious deals") with [unaccountable
leaders](https://theintercept.com/2019/08/13/russia-china-military-africa/
"unaccountable leaders") who give Beijing long-term leases on their nation’s
critical natural resources in exchange for roads, railways, port facilities,
or other infrastructure projects — not exactly a model of free trade in
action.) China is also the top trading partner to [120
nations](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/blog-post/china-top-trading-partner-
more-120-countries "120 nations") worldwide, including key countries in
Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Latin America, alongside a brisk trade with
Europe. This is the lynchpin of China’s global clout.

But U.S. power projection in Hawai‘i and beyond, the entire Pacific strategy,
is based on a different type of projection — the belief that China aspires to
usurp the U.S. as the global hegemon through military might.
[Exaggerating](https://theintercept.com/2024/03/16/tiktok-china-security-
threat/ "Exaggerating") the threat posed by China is a foolproof [marketing
scheme](https://theintercept.com/2026/06/06/anthropic-ai-investor-abu-dhabi-
china/ "marketing scheme") for the weapons contractors, Pentagon bureaucrats,
K-Street lobbyists, and [venture capital
firms](https://theintercept.com/2023/02/03/china-americas-frontier-fund/
"venture capital firms") that [profit
handsomely](https://theintercept.com/2024/03/21/china-tiktok-jacob-helberg-
palantir/ "profit handsomely") from preparations for war with Beijing.

As military budget analyst Stephen Semler has
[documented](https://quincyinst.org/2025/07/08/new-research-military-
contractors-received-over-half-of-pentagon-spending-since-2020/ "documented"),
more than half the Pentagon budget goes to private companies, for everything
from long-range bombers and [intercontinental ballistic
missiles](https://nationalinterest.org/blog/buzz/heres-idea-scrap-americas-
nuclear-armed-icbms-102622 "intercontinental ballistic missiles") to F-35
combat aircraft that are [virtually
useless](https://abcnews.com/Blotter/35-fighter-plan-acquisition-malpractice-
pentagon-official/story?id=15530008 "virtually useless") in modern warfare, to
the [unproven, overhyped](https://harpers.org/archive/2024/03/the-pentagons-
silicon-valley-problem-andrew-cockburn/ "unproven, overhyped") products of the
[Silicon Valley military tech
moguls](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/08/openai-anthropic-military-
contract-ethics-surveillance/ "Silicon Valley military tech moguls"), like the
at least 686 artificial intelligence projects currently being funded by the
Pentagon.

On the military front, China’s ability to challenge the U.S. is grounded in
its [nuclear forces](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/china-and-nuclear-
weapons/ "nuclear forces"), which are much smaller than America’s but are on
the rise in an effort to keep Washington from having a large-enough edge to
wipe out Beijing’s ability to respond to a first strike.

The U.S. may not be able to threaten China’s nuclear deterrent any time soon,
but in the face of the U.S. military build-up in the Pacific, Beijing appears
to be preparing for a [worst-
case](https://www.rand.org/pubs/commentary/2025/10/dont-let-chinese-fears-of-
a-us-decapitation-strike.html "worst-case") scenario. Chinese President Xi
Jinping seems to value nuclear weapons more than his predecessors, who were
content to keep a [few hundred nuclear warheads
](https://www.gmfus.org/news/deciphering-chinas-nuclear-modernization "few
hundred nuclear warheads ")that could reach U.S. soil versus Washington’s much
larger nuclear arsenal. China is also leveraging is technological base,
including its faster pace at training scientists and engineers. This positions
China to [challenge](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/27/opinion/chips-ai-
china-trump.html "challenge") Washington in an [AI arms
race](https://theintercept.com/2019/07/21/ai-race-china-artificial-
intelligence/ "AI arms race").

And yet war is not inevitable, despite what many China hawks constantly
suggest. Returning to a [common
understanding](https://nationalinterest.org/feature/worrisome-erosion-one-
china-policy-206253 "common understanding") on Taiwan — one in which the U.S.
agrees to limit its political recognition of the island or support for
independence in exchange for a Chinese pledge not to seek reunification
through military means — is the best way to avoid a catastrophic conflict. It
would also clear the way for cooperation on urgent issues like addressing the
climate crisis, preventing pandemics, and promoting equitable global
arrangements to reduce poverty and inequality. At the same time, it would make
things safer for hundreds of millions of people from Japan and South Korea to
Guam and Hawai‘i.

**Paying the Price**

America’s military-first approach to China and the world at large comes at a
high price, even when the guns are silent. History demonstrates that merely
preparing for war costs lives, as the fate of victims of Cold War-era nuclear
testing from [New Mexico](https://searchlightnm.org/on-trinity-test-
anniversary-downwinders-advocate-tina-cordova-continues-fight-for-new-
mexicans/ "New Mexico")and [Utah](https://www.downwinders.com/ "Utah") to the
[Marshall Islands](https://www.justsecurity.org/89194/us-policy-on-marshall-
islands-nuclear-test-compensation-must-change-china-is-watching/ "Marshall
Islands") attests. But as Arjun Makhijani, a nuclear engineer and the
president of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research, has pointed
out, the toll of nuclear weapons research, development, and production is
global in scope, creating “[a worldwide archipelago of radioactive
wastelands](https://thebulletin.org/2025/08/the-nuclear-road-not-taken-and-
its-consequences-80-years-after-the-destruction-of-hiroshima-and-
nagasaki/#post-heading "a worldwide archipelago of radioactive wastelands")”
that have cost millions of lives since the dawn of the nuclear age. The
military’s impact on lives and health is also exacerbated by the proliferation
of non-nuclear toxins and [unexploded
ordnance](https://theintercept.com/2025/04/30/vietnam-war-anniversary-
landmines-bombs/ "unexploded ordnance") created by generations of war.

In short, military buildups mean far more than moving money around, although
that too poses serious risks when it comes at the expense of investments in
public health, nutrition, education, and anti-poverty efforts.

Military expansions involve constructing and maintaining new weapons factories
and existing military bases, deploying new weaponry, engaging in costly
training exercises, and, all too often, prosecuting senseless, devastating
wars like the current conflict with
[Iran](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/28/iran-missiles-drones-us-air-
defenses/ "Iran"), the [forever
war](https://theintercept.com/2024/03/07/pentagon-somalia-africa-terrorism-
failure/ "forever war") in
[Somalia](https://theintercept.com/2026/05/27/trump-war-isis-somalia-
sebastian-gorka/ "Somalia"), and a new conflict percolating in
[Ecuador](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/04/us-military-ecuador-trump/
"Ecuador").

The Institute for Policy Studies report, prepared by both mainland and
Hawai‘i-based analysts and advocates, offers a lesson in the perils of
military expansion. Hosting facilities geared toward a future war against
China come at a human and environmental cost that far outstrips the
([routinely overstated](https://ips-dc.org/report-true-cost-of-u-s-military-
bases-in-hawaii/ "routinely overstated")) economic benefits that U.S. military
bases and weapons deployments generate, according to the IPS analysis.

The report reveals that decades of military use of
[PFAS](https://theintercept.com/2020/11/07/military-pfas-pollution-japan/
"PFAS") (known as “forever chemicals”) have contaminated soil, groundwater,
and nearshore waters far beyond the footprint of military bases. Remediation
at just three installations is estimated to cost almost $500 million. A leak
at the Navy’s Red Hill Bulk Fuel Storage Facility — which stored roughly 250
million gallons of jet fuel — in Oʻahu also
[contaminated](https://www.civilbeat.org/category/red-hill/ "contaminated")
the drinking water supply of 93,000 people. Due to these and other
environmental disasters, residents of Hawai‘i have suffered [unnecessary
health risks and mortality](https://ips-dc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/report_true_cost_of_us_military_in_hawaii.pdf
"unnecessary health risks and mortality") and could suffer the effects of
further accidents as preparations for war with China ramp up.

Trading short-term jobs for long-term environmental devastation and
generational health risks is a terrible bargain that would never have been
struck without Hawai‘i’s history as a colonial outpost and a pawn in a
superpower competition over which the people of the islands have had far too
little control. While military bases in the mainland U.S. have also caused
enormous health damage, the sheer extent of Hawai‘i’s territory [occupied by
military facilities](https://www.thenation.com/article/activism/military-
recruiting-hawaii-demilitarization-hpj-jrotc/ "occupied by military
facilities") heightens the impact.

Meanwhile, the archipelago’s longtime status as a floating military base and
the foundation for U.S. power projection in the Pacific makes it a primary
target in any U.S.–China conflict, either in a first strike designed to hobble
a looming U.S. attack or in retaliation once a U.S. intervention begins.

The IPS analysis also found that the Pentagon has [overstated](https://ips-
dc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/report_true_cost_of_us_military_in_hawaii.pdf
"overstated") the military’s supposed $10 billion annual economic benefit to
Hawai‘i by nearly 30 percent. On top of this, Hawai‘i is getting little bang
for the buck. Military spending creates approximately 5.3 jobs per $1 million
invested, compared to 12.3 jobs from the same investment in education, food
production, healthcare, or housing. The researchers also found that the
federal government owes Hawai‘i up to $133.7 billion in back rent on top of
the massive environmental cleanup costs.

A non-militarized plan for Hawai‘i’s economy would supply more jobs and be far
more sustainable than the current approach, according to IPS. And there is a
unique opportunity to change, as two military leases of huge swaths of
Hawaiian territory are set to expire.

Washington needs to thoroughly rethink its narrow, self-defeating approach to
Beijing. A less aggressive, more cooperative posture toward China would help
free Hawaiians politically and economically, and it would open the path to a
safer, more peaceful, more prosperous future. It would also allow for a
rollback of the extensive U.S. military buildups in Guam and the Pacific
islands, activities that mirror and are at times even worse in their
environmental damage and security risks than the situation in Hawai‘i itself.

A less aggressive foreign policy toward China requires the demilitarization of
Hawai‘i and a rollback of America’s costly and ill-conceived buildup in the
Pacific. The IPS report clarifies what is at stake and provides a starting
point for what should be a thorough debate on Hawai‘i’s role in U.S. security
strategy. It is, as one of the authors, Jonathan Kay Kamakawiwoʻole Osorio of
the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, put it: “a blueprint for reclaiming our
nation here, in hope and faith in one another.”

cost-nuclear/ "Visit TomDispatch")._
